theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A senior officer of a government agency that supports small businesses is asked to speak at a chamber of commerce lunch in Mandeville. What should she make sure she knows well first?
options: Each board member's personal views on current politics
The agency's mandate, services and current priorities
The names of every business that has ever complained
The full history of every policy the agency has had

questions.stem: At an inter-agency meeting, a ministry officer is asked whether the ministry will fund a new community centre. The ministry has not yet decided. What should she say?
options: Yes, so that the meeting can end on a positive note
No, since such projects are usually refused
That she personally thinks it is a poor idea
That it is not yet decided and she will report back

questions.stem: What does it mean for an officer to "stay within the brief" when representing the organisation?
options: Keep every speech to five minutes or less
Speak only to people who already support the agency
Speak only on matters he is authorised to cover
Refuse to answer any question from the audience

questions.stem: Before a series of community meetings about a new garbage collection schedule, why does a municipal corporation prepare a set of key messages?
options: So every officer gives the same accurate facts
So that officers need not listen to residents' questions
So that the meetings can be cut to ten minutes each
So the councillors can be blamed if anything goes wrong

questions.stem: Which item is most useful in a briefing pack for an officer representing a ministry at a regional conference?
options: A list of the restaurants close to the conference venue
The officer's own appraisal reports for three years
Copies of all the ministry's files on past conferences
Background, the ministry's position, likely questions

questions.stem: How should a public officer refer to a Government Minister when introducing the Minister at a public function in Jamaica?
options: As "Mister" or "Miss", with the Minister's first name
As "the Honourable" and the Minister's full name
As "His Worship", followed by the Minister's surname
By first name only, to make the event feel friendly

questions.stem: At a parish function, which form of address is normally used for the Mayor?
options: The Honourable
Your Excellency
His or Her Worship
The Most Honourable

questions.stem: At a community meeting before a general election, a resident asks a public officer which party's plan for the area is better. What should the officer do?
options: Decline to give a party view and explain the agency's services
Give her personal view, since the meeting is after office hours
Say which party she supports so residents know where she stands
End the meeting at once and leave the community centre

questions.stem: After an officer gives a talk to a business association, the association offers him an expensive watch. What should he do?
options: Accept it, as refusing would offend the association
Decline or declare it, as the code of conduct requires
Accept it and pass it to a family member as a present
Accept it as long as no one saw it being handed over

questions.stem: An agency officer is asked to represent the agency on a panel choosing a local business for a promotion award. Her brother owns one of the businesses. What should she do?
options: Take part, but score her brother's business a little lower
Take part, since several people make the panel's decision
Ask her brother to withdraw from the award without saying why
Declare the interest and step aside from that decision

questions.stem: A journalist comes to an agency's expo booth and asks the officer on duty about a rumoured cut in the agency's budget. What should the officer do?
options: Refer the journalist to the communications unit
Confirm the rumour, as the public has a right to know
Deny the rumour, although she does not know the facts
Give a comment off the record that cannot be quoted

questions.stem: At a public meeting in Port Antonio, a resident asks a detailed question about a road project that the officer cannot answer. What is the best reply?
options: Give a rough guess so the resident is not left without an answer
Say that the question is not relevant to the meeting's topic
Promise to find out and reply by a set date, taking his details
Suggest that the resident writes to the newspaper about it

questions.stem: During a community forum, a resident angrily says the agency has ignored his complaints for months. How should the officer representing the agency respond?
options: Tell him that shouting will not be tolerated at the forum
Explain that the complaints unit is not her responsibility
Argue that the agency has done more than any other agency
Stay calm, accept his frustration, offer to follow up

questions.stem: An officer posts photos from an agency event on her personal social media page and adds her own critical comments on the Minister's policy. What is the main concern?
options: The photos may not be of good enough quality
It may be read as the agency's view and break policy
Her friends may not understand the agency's work
Posting about work events is never allowed at all

questions.stem: A unit in a ministry designs its own flyer, using a stretched copy of the ministry's logo and new colours. What should the unit manager do?
options: Approve it, as a fresh look will catch more attention
Approve it if only a small number will be printed
Have it redone to follow the ministry's brand guidelines
Remove the logo so the flyer cannot be linked to the ministry

questions.stem: Why must an agency's brochure about its grant programme be checked carefully before it is printed?
options: Wrong details mislead the public and harm trust
Brochures are the only way the public learns of grants
Printers refuse any job that has a spelling mistake
Checking gives staff something useful to do when quiet

questions.stem: Which step best makes an agency's public information easy for more citizens to reach and understand?
options: Using technical terms so that it sounds expert
Publishing it only on the agency's own website
Printing it in very small type to save on paper costs
Using plain language and several formats and channels

questions.stem: A government agency will have a booth at a national trade expo in Kingston. What should the team decide first?
options: The colour of the tablecloth for the booth
What it wants to achieve, and with whom
Which staff would like a day out of the office
How many free pens to give to each visitor

questions.stem: An agency spent J$450,000 on its booth at a trade expo and recorded 300 serious enquiries. What was the cost per enquiry?
Which measure best shows whether an agency's booth at a careers fair met its aim of recruiting trainees?
options: The number of flyers printed before the fair
The number of staff who worked at the booth
The number of applications received from the fair
The number of photos of the booth posted online

questions.stem: After representing a ministry at a regional meeting, what should the officer do?
options: Keep the notes until someone asks about the meeting
Post a summary of the private talks on social media
Tell colleagues over lunch what happened at the meeting

questions.stem: Why should an officer who represents her agency on a parish development committee build good relationships with the other members?
options: So the agency can avoid doing its share of the work
So they can work together and settle issues early
So that one of the members may offer her a job
So that the committee always agrees with the agency

questions.stem: A customer service officer is rude to a member of the public, and a video of it spreads online. What does this show most clearly?
options: Every officer's conduct affects the organisation's name
Only the communications unit looks after reputation

questions.stem: An officer will represent her agency at a formal function at King's House. Which is the best preparation for her personal presentation?
options: Wear casual clothes so that she seems approachable
Wear whatever is comfortable, as it is after hours
Check the dress code and the protocol in advance
Ask a colleague to go instead so she can avoid it

questions.stem: At a regional conference, what is the main purpose of networking for an officer who represents a public body?
options: To collect as many business cards as possible
To build contacts that help the body meet its aims
To find a better-paid job in another organisation
To learn other countries' plans for the officer's own use

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a public body's citizens' charter?
options: To list the names of the body's senior managers
To set out the body's rules for staff discipline
To record the minutes of the body's board meetings
To tell the public what service standards to expect

questions.stem: During an outreach event about road safety, residents raise several concerns about their water supply. What should the agency's representatives do with these concerns?
options: Ignore them, as the event was about another topic
Promise quick fixes so that residents leave happy
Record them and pass them on to the right body
Tell residents to phone the head office's main line

questions.stem: An officer is asked to write the agency's entry for a business directory. What should guide the content?
options: Approved, accurate facts on services and contacts
Comparisons showing that other agencies are less helpful
The officer's own opinion of the agency's best services
Promises of services the agency may offer in the future

questions.stem: An officer has 10 minutes to present the agency's services to a group of farmers in St Elizabeth. Which approach is best?
options: Read the agency's annual report aloud from the start
Show 40 slides full of figures as fast as possible
Use technical terms so the agency sounds expert

questions.stem: While representing the ministry at a business forum, an officer is asked about a contract that is still being negotiated. What should she do?
options: Share the details, since the forum is a friendly audience
Say she cannot discuss it while talks are going on
Hint at the likely winner to keep the audience interested
Give the figures off the record to one trusted business owner

questions.stem: A director cannot attend a stakeholder meeting and sends her deputy instead. How should the director prepare the deputy?
options: Tell the deputy to agree to whatever the stakeholders want
Send the deputy without a briefing to test her skills
Brief her on the aims, positions and her limits
Ask the deputy to stay silent for the whole meeting

questions.stem: Which activity would best promote a parish municipal corporation's new recycling programme to residents?
options: Demonstrations at markets and schools, with simple leaflets
One notice in the corporation's internal staff newsletter
A long technical report placed on the corporation's website
A private briefing for the councillors and senior managers

questions.stem: What should a public body decide before it chooses the channels for a promotional campaign?
options: The font to be used in its letters
The target audience and the message
The names of the campaign staff
The date of the next board meeting

questions.stem: An agency has J$1,200,000 for a promotion. It plans to spend 40% on radio, 35% on social media and the rest on printed material. How much is left for printed material?
Who should normally post on an agency's official social media pages?
options: Officers authorised by the communications policy
Any officer who happens to know the account password
The agency's IT supplier, using its own judgement
Members of the public who follow the page

questions.stem: An officer is part of a delegation meeting international donors. One donor criticises Jamaica's progress on a programme. What should the officer do?
options: Agree in public that the programme has failed
Argue that the donor does not understand Jamaica
Reply calmly with facts and refer policy points to the head
Leave the meeting to show the remark gave offence

questions.stem: Which behaviour best shows public service values when an officer deals with the public at an outreach event?
options: Serving people the officer knows personally first
Treating every person with courtesy, fairness and respect
Spending more time with people who praise the agency
Avoiding people who look as if they may complain

questions.stem: At an inter-agency meeting, an officer agrees that her agency will supply some data by the end of the month. What should she do afterwards?
options: Wait for the other agency to remind her before acting
Assume her manager will hear about it from someone else
Send the data only if the other agency asks twice
Record the promise, tell her manager and see it is kept

questions.stem: Visitors to an agency's booth were asked to rate the information they received. Of the 250 who replied, 200 rated it useful. What percentage is this?
Why does an organisation train all front-line staff, and not only managers, to promote its services?
options: Front-line staff are the people the public meets most
Managers are not allowed to speak to the public at all
Training front-line staff costs the agency nothing
Front-line staff decide the organisation's policies

questions.stem: A manager wants a campaign poster to say the agency processes all permits "in 24 hours", but most take five days. What should the officer preparing the poster do?
options: Use the claim, as nobody takes posters literally
Use the claim, with tiny print about possible delays
Use the claim only on posters outside Kingston
Raise the concern and suggest a claim that is true

questions.stem: Which is NOT appropriate when an officer represents the agency at a public event?
options: Wearing the agency's identification badge
Using a colleague's personal problems as an example
Using the agency's approved key messages
Taking contact details to follow up questions

questions.stem: At a community meeting, a resident tells an agency officer that another officer asked her for money to speed up her application. What should the officer do?
options: Take the details and report it through the proper channel
Tell the resident that such things happen in every agency
Challenge the other officer about it in front of the public
Advise the resident to pay so her application moves faster

questions.stem: An officer sits on a national committee as her agency's representative. The committee is about to vote on a matter on which her agency has a clear, agreed position. How should she vote?
options: As she personally prefers, since the vote is secret
With the majority, to avoid any disagreement
In line with the agency's agreed position
She should not vote on any matter at all

questions.stem: After each outreach event, an agency team meets to discuss what worked and what did not. What is the main benefit?
options: It gives the team a reason to stay late after events
Lessons learned are used to improve the next event
It removes the need to report to the director
It decides which officer is to blame for problems

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one word names the official purpose and powers given to a public body, usually by law?
What term describes a situation where an officer's private interests could affect, or seem to affect, their official duties?
What is the name of the document that sets out how an organisation's logo, colours and fonts must be used?
What term describes a short, clear summary of an organisation's work that can be given in about 30 seconds?
What one word describes how the public, partners and others see and judge an organisation?
What is the title of the person authorised to speak to the media on behalf of an organisation?
Give the two-letter abbreviation for the work of managing an organisation's relationship and reputation with the public.
An agency planned to reach 1,200 people through outreach events this quarter and actually reached 1,500. What percentage of the target did it achieve?
Of 12 news stories about an agency's campaign, 9 were positive. What percentage of the stories were positive?
What word is used for a public body's activities that take information and services out into communities?
What is the name of the document that sets the standards of behaviour expected of public officers, including rules on gifts?
When several dignitaries attend a function, what term describes the accepted order in which they are ranked, seated and introduced?
What is the name of the short statement of an organisation's core purpose that representatives often quote?
What term describes a public officer's duty not to take sides in party politics while doing official work?
An outreach team held 6 community events at a total cost of J$540,000. What was the average cost per event? Give the answer in J$.

essays.stem: Your agency, which helps small businesses register and find finance, will have a booth at a three-day national expo in Kingston. Plan how you will represent and promote the agency at the expo.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would set clear aims, for example 400 serious enquiries and 120 business registrations started at the booth, and identify the target audience: new and small business owners, especially young people and women in business. I would agree key messages with the communications unit, such as how to register, the finance available and where to get help, and make sure all printed and digital materials follow the brand guidelines and are accurate and in plain language. I would plan the booth layout, with a laptop for on-the-spot registration, short demonstrations and a sign-up sheet that collects contact details with consent. I would choose a team of officers who know the services well, brief them on the messages, their limits of authority and how to handle media and difficult questions, and set a rota so each has breaks. I would prepare a budget in J$ and a checklist of equipment. During the expo we would record enquiries daily. Afterwards, I would follow up every lead within a week, work out the cost per enquiry and write a report with lessons for next year.
markingPoints: Sets measurable aims and identifies the target audience
Agrees accurate key messages and materials that follow brand guidelines
Plans the booth, staffing, briefing and limits of authority
Collects contacts properly and records enquiries
Follows up, evaluates (e.g. cost per enquiry) and reports lessons

essays.stem: You will represent your ministry at an inter-agency meeting where a disputed issue, the sharing of costs for a new drainage scheme, will be discussed. Describe how you would prepare and how you would conduct yourself at the meeting.
essays.modelAnswer: To prepare, I would read the agenda and all past papers and minutes on the drainage scheme, and find out the ministry's agreed position and the limits of what I may agree to. I would get this in a short written brief from my director, with the figures for the costs, the reasons for our position and any fallback options she has approved. I would think about the other agencies' interests and likely objections, and prepare clear answers and questions. I would check the facts with the finance unit so I do not give wrong figures. At the meeting I would arrive on time, introduce myself and my role, and present the ministry's position politely and clearly. I would listen carefully to others, ask questions to understand their concerns, and look for common ground. If a proposal goes beyond my brief, I would say that I must take it back to the ministry rather than agree on the spot. I would avoid personal opinions and keep confidential matters private. I would note all decisions and actions, and afterwards write a report for my director with the outcomes and follow-ups.
markingPoints: Reads papers and obtains the ministry's position and limits of authority in writing
Checks facts and anticipates other agencies' views
Presents the position clearly and courteously, and listens
Does not go beyond the brief; refers new proposals back
Records outcomes and reports back afterwards

essays.stem: Explain how political neutrality and the code of conduct guide a public officer who represents the organisation in public, using examples on gifts, conflicts of interest and personal opinions.
essays.modelAnswer: A public officer represents the organisation and the Government of the day, not a political party or their own interests. Political neutrality means the officer serves the public fairly whatever their party, explains policies accurately and does not campaign, take sides or share party views while acting officially. For example, at a community meeting before an election, the officer should decline to say which party's plan is better and stick to the agency's services. The code of conduct sets rules on gifts: an officer offered an expensive gift after giving a talk should decline it or declare it as the code requires, because accepting could look like a reward that affects future decisions. On conflicts of interest, an officer whose relative is involved in a matter, such as a business entered for an award, must declare the interest and step aside. On personal opinions, the officer should not criticise the Minister's policy in public or on social media, because the comment may be taken as the agency's view. These rules protect public trust, which is the organisation's most valuable asset.
markingPoints: Explains political neutrality correctly
Gives a correct example on gifts (decline or declare)
Gives a correct example on conflict of interest (declare and step aside)
Explains limits on personal opinions, including social media
Links the rules to public trust in the organisation

essays.stem: You are representing a municipal corporation at a community meeting in Spanish Town about a delayed road repair. Many residents are angry. Explain how you would handle the meeting.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting I would get the facts: the reason for the delay, the new timetable, what the corporation can and cannot promise, and who is responsible. I would agree key messages with my manager and bring an engineer if possible. At the start I would introduce myself, thank residents for coming, and set out the purpose and ground rules, such as one person speaking at a time. I would acknowledge that residents have been inconvenienced and apologise for the delay without blaming others. I would give the facts clearly and honestly, including the new dates, and explain what is being done. When residents speak angrily, I would stay calm, listen without interrupting, and show I understand their frustration. I would answer what I can and, where I cannot, promise to find out and reply by a set date. I would not make promises outside my authority or give political views. A colleague would record all concerns and contact details. At the end I would summarise the main points and next steps. Afterwards I would report to my manager and make sure residents receive the promised replies.
markingPoints: Prepares facts, key messages and limits of authority
Sets the purpose and ground rules and acknowledges residents' frustration
Stays calm, listens and gives honest, clear information
Avoids promises beyond authority and political views; follows up unanswered questions
Records concerns, summarises next steps and reports back

essays.stem: An agency ran a J$2,400,000 campaign to promote a new online application service. Website visits rose from 8,000 a month before the campaign to 20,000 during it, and 600 applications were received against a target of 500. Evaluate the campaign and say what further information you would want.
essays.modelAnswer: The campaign appears successful. Website visits rose by 12,000 a month, which is 150% more than before. Applications reached 600, which is 120% of the target of 500. The cost per application was J$2,400,000 divided by 600, or J$4,000. To judge whether this is good value, I would compare it with the cost of handling paper applications and with earlier campaigns. However, the figures do not tell the whole story. I would want to know how many applications were complete and approved, not just received, and whether applicants came from the target groups, such as rural residents and small businesses. I would want to know which channels, such as radio, social media or community meetings, brought in most applicants, so future spending can focus on them. I would check whether the visits continued after the campaign ended. I would also look at complaints and feedback about the online service, since promotion can attract people to a service that then lets them down. With this information I would recommend whether to repeat the campaign.
markingPoints: Calculates the rise in visits (12,000, or 150%) correctly
Calculates achievement against target (120%) and cost per application (J$4,000) correctly
Judges value for money by comparison
Identifies further information needed (quality of applications, target groups, channels, lasting effect)
Considers feedback and makes a recommendation

essays.stem: Compare four channels a public body could use to promote a new pension information service, and recommend a mix to reach rural seniors and young urban workers.
essays.modelAnswer: Radio reaches many people, including older people in rural areas, and works well for short, repeated messages, but it cannot carry much detail and costs money for air time. Social media is cheap, fast and reaches young urban workers, and it allows two-way questions, but it reaches fewer older people and comments must be monitored. Community meetings, held in churches, community centres or markets, allow face-to-face explanation and questions and build trust, especially with seniors, but they reach only small numbers and need staff time. Printed leaflets and posters at post offices, health centres and parish offices can be kept and reread, but they may be ignored and must be kept up to date. For rural seniors I would recommend radio and community meetings, supported by large-print leaflets at places they visit. For young urban workers I would recommend social media with short videos, plus messages through employers. All channels would carry the same key messages and contact details, and I would track enquiries by channel to see which works best.
markingPoints: Describes four suitable channels
Gives a strength and a weakness of each
Matches channels to rural seniors with reasons
Matches channels to young urban workers with reasons
Keeps messages consistent and tracks results by channel

essays.stem: Explain why every staff member is an ambassador for a public body, and describe how a manager can help staff represent the body well.
essays.modelAnswer: Most members of the public form their view of a public body from the officer they meet at the counter, on the phone, at an event or online, not from its annual report. A helpful, courteous officer builds trust, while one rude encounter, especially if it is filmed and shared, can damage the body's reputation widely. Staff also represent the body outside work, for example on social media or in the community. A manager can help by making sure every officer understands the body's mission, services and values, through induction and regular briefings. Staff should be given up-to-date information and key messages so they can answer questions accurately. Training in customer service, handling complaints and difficult questions, and the code of conduct gives them confidence. The manager should explain the rules on speaking to the media, social media and political neutrality. Uniforms or ID badges and tidy work areas support a professional image. The manager should lead by example, recognise officers who represent the body well, and deal fairly with poor conduct. Feedback from the public can be shared to keep improving.
markingPoints: Explains that the public judges the body by its officers' conduct
Notes that staff represent the body outside work, including online
Gives staff knowledge of the mission, services and key messages
Trains staff and explains rules on media, social media and neutrality
Leads by example, recognises good practice and uses feedback

essays.stem: Your agency is hosting the opening of a new office in a parish. The Minister, the Mayor and the Custos will attend. Describe the protocol arrangements you would make.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start early by confirming who will attend and their correct titles, and by checking the order of precedence, using the ministry's protocol officer or official guidance where unsure. Invitations would be sent in good time with correct titles, and attendance confirmed. I would plan the programme with timings and agree who speaks and in what order, normally ending with the most senior guest or the person who officially opens the office. Seating would follow the order of precedence, with name cards, and reserved places for other guests such as councillors and community leaders. I would arrange for a named officer to meet each dignitary on arrival and escort them. The master of ceremonies would be briefed on titles and correct pronunciation of names, for example "the Honourable" for the Minister and "His Worship" or "Her Worship" for the Mayor. I would check details such as the national anthem, a prayer, the flag, the ribbon and photography. Security and accessibility would be planned. After the event, thank-you letters would be sent to the dignitaries.
markingPoints: Confirms attendees, correct titles and the order of precedence, seeking expert advice
Plans the programme and speaking order
Arranges seating and the reception and escort of dignitaries
Briefs the master of ceremonies on titles and names
Covers details such as anthem, flag, security, and sends thanks afterwards

essays.stem: You have been appointed to represent your agency on a national steering committee. Explain your responsibilities to your agency and to the committee, and how you would keep your agency informed.
essays.modelAnswer: My first responsibility to my agency is to present its agreed positions accurately and to protect its interests, within the limits of authority my director gives me. Before each meeting I would read the papers, consult the relevant units, and agree the agency's position on each item, getting written guidance on anything sensitive. I must not commit the agency to costs or actions beyond my authority without approval. My responsibility to the committee is to take part constructively, attend regularly, prepare, listen to others and help the committee reach good decisions for the public. I must respect the committee's confidentiality and declare any conflict of interest. If the agency's position conflicts with the committee's direction, I should explain the position honestly and take the issue back to my director rather than act alone. To keep the agency informed, I would write a short report after each meeting on the decisions, actions for the agency and deadlines, and send it to my director and the units affected. I would track the agency's actions to make sure commitments are met, and give a fuller report each quarter.
markingPoints: Presents the agency's agreed positions within limits of authority
Prepares by reading papers and consulting units
Takes part constructively and respects confidentiality and conflicts of interest
Refers conflicts between agency and committee back to the director
Reports back after each meeting and tracks commitments

essays.stem: Recommend the main points of a policy on how staff of a public body represent the body on social media, and justify each point.
essays.modelAnswer: First, only staff authorised by the communications unit may post on the body's official accounts, so that messages are accurate, approved and consistent. Second, official posts must follow the brand guidelines and use plain, respectful language, because they represent the body to the whole public. Third, staff using personal accounts must not present their views as the body's views, and should make clear that opinions are their own if they mention their work, because readers may otherwise take a comment as official. Fourth, staff must not post confidential information, personal data about citizens or colleagues, or photos taken at work without permission, in line with the data protection law and the code of conduct. Fifth, public officers must stay politically neutral and must not attack the Government's policies or other people online, because this damages trust in the public service. Sixth, staff who see false information or abuse about the body should report it to the communications unit rather than reply themselves, so the response is measured. Finally, the policy should explain the consequences of breaches and be reviewed each year.
markingPoints: Limits official posting to authorised staff, with a reason
Sets rules for personal accounts and separating personal views
Protects confidential and personal data in line with the law
Requires political neutrality and respectful conduct online
Sets reporting routes, consequences and review, each justified

practical1.title: Plan and staff an information booth for a public body
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up public body (for example a parish municipal corporation promoting a new recycling programme, or an agency promoting a training grant), with its mandate, services, brand guidelines and a budget in J$. As a group, plan and set up an information booth, then staff it while the assessor and other trainees visit as members of the public. Each member has a named role: booth manager (writes the one-page plan with aims, target audience, budget and how success will be measured); messages officer (writes the key messages sheet and a list of likely questions with approved answers); materials designer (makes a poster or flyer that follows the brand guidelines and uses plain language); outreach officer (designs the visitor sign-up and feedback form, collecting contact details only with consent); and evaluation officer (records enquiries during the visit session and writes a short evaluation, including the cost per enquiry from the assessor's figures). In a group of four, the booth manager also does the evaluation. During the 40-minute visit session, every member must speak with visitors, and each must deal with at least one difficult question from a role card.
materials: Case pack and brand guidelines from the assessor
A table, display board or flipchart for the booth
Computer and printer, or card, paper and markers
Templates for the plan, sign-up form and evaluation
photos: The one-page booth plan with aims, audience, budget and measures
The key messages sheet with likely questions and answers
The poster or flyer next to the brand guidelines
The completed sign-up and feedback forms (with names covered) and the evaluation
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The plan has clear, measurable aims and a target audience
Key messages and materials are accurate, in plain language and follow the brand guidelines
Spoke courteously with visitors and stayed within the body's approved messages
Handled a difficult question calmly, without guessing or giving political views
Collected contact details only with consent
Evaluation uses the figures correctly and gives lessons for next time
safety: Collect only made-up contact details during the exercise, and hand all forms to the assessor at the end
Treat every visitor with courtesy and respect
Set up the booth so cables and boards do not cause trips or falls
Share the workload fairly and take a short break after the visit session

practical2.title: Represent the organisation at a meeting and report back
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a public body must send a representative to a community or inter-agency meeting about a disputed issue (for example a planned bus terminus in a busy town centre). Part A (45 minutes): the group prepares a written briefing note for the representative, setting out background, the body's position, the limits of authority, key messages and likely questions with answers. Part B (30 minutes): role-play the meeting. Each member has a named role: representative (presents the body's position and answers questions); chair (runs the meeting and keeps order); two stakeholders, such as a vendors' association leader and a resident, who use role cards from the assessor; and a note-taker (records questions, answers and commitments). In a group of four, the chair also takes notes. Part C (45 minutes): the representative and note-taker write a one-page back-to-office report with outcomes, commitments and follow-ups; the other members each write the reply letter to one stakeholder's unanswered question, for the director's signature. Then swap roles and run a second, shorter meeting so that a second member acts as representative.
materials: Case card and role cards from the assessor
Briefing note, meeting notes and back-to-office report templates
A room set up for a meeting
Computer and printer, or paper and pens
photos: The written briefing note with position, limits and likely questions
The meeting in progress, showing the set-up (faces only if all agree)
The note-taker's record of the meeting
checklist: The briefing note sets out the position, key messages and limits of authority clearly
The representative presented the position accurately and courteously
Stayed within the brief and referred matters beyond it back to the body
Listened to stakeholders and handled disagreement calmly and neutrally
Notes and the back-to-office report record commitments accurately
Reply letters are accurate, polite and use plain language
safety: Use only the made-up case; do not discuss real officers, residents or disputes
Keep the role play respectful, and stop if anyone becomes uncomfortable
Keep notes confidential to the group and the assessor
Photograph faces only if every person agrees and the Centre allows it
